package_info.package_manager: system (Linux distribution package managers: dpkg, rpm, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a highly sophisticated backdoor introduced through a malicious build process. This process modifies the liblzma library to enable remote code execution and SSH authentication bypass on affected Linux systems. The backdoor leverages advanced techniques, such as glibc IFUNC resolvers and audit hooks, to intercept and replace cryptographic functions (specifically RSA_public_decrypt), allowing attackers to gain unauthorized access to systems using the compromised library. The malicious modifications are present only in release tarballs, not in the upstream source repository, making detection more difficult.

execution_context.trigger: build-time (during package compilation on target system)
execution_context.file_location: build-to-host.m4 (malicious M4 macro file in tarball, not in git repo)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: M4 macro logic that extracts and injects malicious object code into the build process, targeting x86-64 Linux with glibc and GCC, and only when built via dpkg or rpm.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build-time, the code checks for x86-64 architecture, glibc, GCC, and the presence of dpkg or rpm build environments, then extracts and injects a hidden malicious object file into the liblzma binary, resulting in a compromised shared library.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The build-to-host.m4 file is only present in the release tarball and not in the upstream source repository, indicating intentional concealment. Its logic is designed to conditionally inject a malicious object file only on specific systems, evading detection during normal development and review processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard build scripts should not inject hidden object code or alter binaries based on the build environment in an undocumented manner. This behavior violates the expectation of transparent, auditable, and reproducible builds.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Conditional compilation is legitimate for platform-specific optimizations, but not for injecting undocumented or hidden object code that is not present in the source repository.
key_indicators: Presence of build-to-host.m4 only in release tarball
Conditional logic targeting x86-64, glibc, GCC, and dpkg/rpm environments
Injection of object code not present in upstream source repository
Build artifacts differ from source-controlled builds

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when liblzma is loaded, e.g., via sshd with systemd patch)
execution_context.file_location: liblzma.so (compiled shared library, after build-time injection)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code leveraging glibc IFUNC mechanism to add a resolver for crc64_resolve, which installs a glibc audit hook to intercept and replace the RSA_public_decrypt function in OpenSSH.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C (compiled to object code, injected via build process)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the compromised liblzma shared library is loaded (such as by sshd via libsystemd), the code uses a glibc IFUNC resolver to install a glibc audit hook, intercepting calls to RSA_public_decrypt and replacing them with a malicious implementation that enables authentication bypass or remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a glibc IFUNC resolver and audit hook to intercept cryptographic functions is highly unusual and only makes sense for malicious purposes, especially in a compression library. This technique allows the attacker to hijack cryptographic operations in unrelated processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Compression libraries like liblzma are not expected to interact with cryptographic functions or install audit hooks that affect unrelated system components. Such behavior is a clear violation of the principle of least privilege and separation of concerns.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Audit hooks may be used for debugging or profiling in development environments, but never for replacing cryptographic functions in production libraries, especially not in a compression library.
key_indicators: IFUNC resolver for unrelated function (crc64_resolve) present in liblzma.so
Installation of glibc audit hook from within a compression library
Replacement of RSA_public_decrypt in OpenSSH context
Unexpected code sections or symbols in liblzma.so

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a specially crafted compressed test file is processed)
execution_context.file_location: liblzma test files (maliciously crafted, embedded in package)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Maliciously crafted compressed test files that, when processed, trigger the backdoor logic in the injected code.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a maliciously crafted compressed test file is processed by the library, it triggers the backdoor logic in the injected code, activating the IFUNC resolver and audit hook installation, which enables authentication bypass or remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Test files are being used to trigger hidden code paths and activate the backdoor logic, which is a clear abuse of the test infrastructure. This allows the attacker to activate the backdoor only under specific, controlled conditions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Test files are expected to validate library functionality, not to serve as triggers for hidden or malicious code. Using test files as activation mechanisms for backdoors is a severe violation of trust.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for test files to trigger hidden code paths or activate backdoors in production libraries.
key_indicators: Test files act as triggers for hidden code in liblzma
Activation of backdoor logic only when specific files are processed
Presence of non-standard or undocumented test files in the package

attack_chain.action: Malicious build-to-host.m4 file is included in the release tarball and triggers during package build on targeted systems.
attack_chain.leads_to: Injection of malicious object code into liblzma binary

attack_chain.action: Injected object code leverages glibc IFUNC to install a glibc audit hook at runtime when liblzma is loaded (e.g., via libsystemd in sshd).
attack_chain.leads_to: Interception and replacement of RSA_public_decrypt in OpenSSH

attack_chain.action: Maliciously crafted compressed test files are processed, triggering the backdoor logic in the injected code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Activation of authentication bypass or remote code execution in sshd

attack_chain.action: Attacker authenticates to the compromised SSH server using a crafted RSA key, bypassing normal authentication.
attack_chain.leads_to: Unauthorized remote access or code execution on the target system

behavioral_signatures: Presence of build scripts or files in release tarballs not present in source control (e.g., build-to-host.m4)
Conditional injection of object code during build targeting x86-64, glibc, GCC, and dpkg/rpm environments
Use of glibc IFUNC resolvers and audit hooks in non-cryptographic libraries such as liblzma
Interception or replacement of cryptographic functions (e.g., RSA_public_decrypt) by unrelated libraries
Activation of hidden code paths when processing specific, maliciously crafted test files
file_indicators: build-to-host.m4 present in release tarball but not in upstream git repository
liblzma.so binaries with unexpected object code sections or IFUNC/audit hook symbols
Maliciously crafted compressed test files embedded in the package
network_indicators: Unusual authentication attempts to sshd from external sources, especially using crafted RSA keys
Potential exfiltration or command-and-control traffic if attacker leverages remote code execution
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Compare release tarballs to upstream source repositories to identify unexpected files such as build-to-host.m4. Analyze build logs for evidence of conditional object code injection. Inspect liblzma.so binaries for the presence of IFUNC resolvers and audit hooks, and for unexpected symbols or code sections. Monitor for libraries intercepting cryptographic functions, particularly RSA_public_decrypt, in unrelated processes. Scan for the presence of maliciously crafted test files within the package. Monitor SSH authentication logs for unusual patterns, such as successful logins with previously unseen RSA keys or from unexpected sources, especially on systems running affected liblzma versions.
